setup.panel.title: Three flags
setup.panel.description: Three files are waiting in the kata/step2/java folder, exactly one for each kind of instruction this unit covered. No script prints them and no build generates them. You find them simply by opening the project and reading the files.
setup.panel.wrong: Not that one. Copy it exactly, braces and all.
setup.flag.skill.label: The procedure
setup.flag.skill.hint: A fixed way of working that this project wants followed in exactly the same way on every interaction. The file sits in the standard location where the agent loads it automatically, unasked, at the start.
setup.flag.skill.help: It is a skill, and the section above gives you its shape: a folder, a file with frontmatter, a description saying when to reach for it. This project ships one, so start by asking your agent what that project carries in the way of skills. If you would rather come at it from the other end, ask it inside kata/step2/java what it must do before writing a line of Javadoc: an agent that answers with a house rule has read the file, and you can ask it which file that was.
setup.flag.module.label: The initial project context
setup.flag.module.hint: The context the project gives the agent before you type a question or command yourself, at the very top of the project.
setup.flag.module.help: It is the file this unit spends most of its words on, and there is one at the top of kata/step2/java. That is what an agent reads first when a session starts in that folder, so open it yourself and read it the way the agent would, top to bottom. Somewhere in there is a line that hands the flag over.
setup.flag.package.label: The specific instruction
setup.flag.package.hint: The same kind of instruction file as above, but placed deeper in the folder structure so that it applies only to one specific package instead of the whole project.
setup.flag.package.help: This kind of file is scoped: it joins the context only once the agent goes into the folder that holds it, so this one is never read while you work at the top of the project. Go down into the source tree until you reach a package whose rules would need saying, and look for a second copy of the same file there. Failing that, ask your agent to list every one of them under kata/step2/java and compare the list against what you already have.
workshop.panel.title: Where they land
workshop.panel.description: Paste each flag as a build, an endpoint or a native image hands it over. Each one is leetspeak between curly braces, and the browser checks it here.
workshop.panel.wrong: Not that one. Read the flag straight from the output it came in.
workshop.flag.coverage.label: Coverage floor
workshop.flag.coverage.hint: Ninety percent line coverage on the loans module. The web and config layers are left out, and so is the code the last two flags ask you to write.
workshop.flag.coverage.help: This is the goal-shaped one, so hand it over as an outcome rather than a test list: ninety percent, mvn verify -Pgraded after every class, no public signature changed. The unit on spending tokens argues that shape. If you keep correcting the tests that come back, the prompt was fine. The skill from the pre-flight was missing.
workshop.flag.complexity.label: Complexity ceiling
workshop.flag.complexity.hint: No method above a cyclomatic complexity of ten.
workshop.flag.complexity.help: Hand over the ceiling, not a refactor plan, and name the check it runs after each class. The unit on craft is the shape of the fix: every decision in a small method of its own. If your agent keeps splitting the method the wrong way, that boundary belongs in CLAUDE.md rather than in your next three messages.
workshop.flag.honest.label: Honest coverage
workshop.flag.honest.hint: Eighty percent of mutations caught: tests that can actually fail.
workshop.flag.honest.help: This is the row that does not move when you add tests, and now is the moment to find out why. Coverage is a proxy: a hundred percent of the lines can run under tests that assert nothing, and the number stays green. So the build changes the domain in small ways, runs your tests again, and scores how many of those changes your suite caught. Put the goal on that score and ask for the exact fee each case returns. Asking for tests that assert something is a correction you will keep typing, and the patterns unit puts a correction like that in the skill rather than in another message.
workshop.flag.statement.label: Statement endpoint
workshop.flag.statement.hint: Build the method the failing tests describe, then read the code the endpoint returns.
workshop.flag.statement.help: Plan mode, against a spec you did not write. Run mvn test -Pchallenge, have your agent read the failures and plan MemberStatements.forTier before it writes anything, then read the plan back against the test method names one at a time. A plan that answers the first name and skips the fourth is the failure this row exists for. Then start the service and call the endpoint.
workshop.flag.native.label: Native image
workshop.flag.native.hint: Plan a native image of step 2 that keeps its flag resource. A one-shot compiles and comes up empty.
workshop.flag.native.help: Boot's parent pom already carries the native profile, so mvn -Pnative native:compile is the whole build, and it needs a GraalVM JDK on your PATH. Plan mode tells you what an ahead-of-time image leaves behind before you spend the minutes. Spend them once, run the binary, and read what it prints where the flag should be. If it will not start at all, something else is holding its port.
run-sheet.pair.name: Two jobs, neither waits
run-sheet.description: The capstone in four stages: what you hand over at each, the commands that answer, and the flags each one pays out.
run-sheet.preflight.name: Pre-flight
run-sheet.preflight.hand: The project, before the first message.
run-sheet.goal.name: One goal, three flags
run-sheet.build.name: Build what is missing
run-sheet.build.hand: A plan, against somebody else's tests.
run-sheet.compile.name: Compile it down
run-sheet.compile.hand: An outcome you cannot iterate your way to.
run-sheet.debrief.name: Debrief
run-sheet.debrief.hand: Your own diff, back to the agent.
set-up-first.title: Set it up first
set-up-first.description: Ten minutes on kata/step2/java before a line of the module changes. Note the time you start; the debrief asks where it went.
set-up-first.red.label: Run mvn verify -Pgraded once, untouched, and read the rows it prints.
set-up-first.command.label: Have your agent read the project and put that command in kata/step2/java/CLAUDE.md as the check that validates this work.
set-up-first.hook.label: Wire the same command as a Stop hook in settings.json, so it runs whether or not the agent remembers to.
set-up-first.gaps.label: Add the ## Gaps rule, so a run stops at something nobody decided instead of picking the likeliest answer.
set-up-first.skill.label: Turn the test conventions this project already uses into a skill: AssertJ, one @ParameterizedTest per table of cases.
look-at-afternoon.title: Look at the afternoon
look-at-afternoon.description: Once the flags are in. None of these earns one, and none of them is graded; the tick is a bookmark.
look-at-afternoon.audit.label: Point the agent at your own diff and ask for audit.md as a table, then close its worst row and run the graded build again.
look-at-afternoon.count.label: Split the time you noted four ways: setting up, waiting on builds, reading diffs, and deciding.
look-at-afternoon.keep.label: Take the correction you typed more than twice and write it into the skill, where it arrives before the next mistake.
look-at-afternoon.asked.label: If no run stopped to ask you anything, go back through the diff for the decision it made instead.
where.title: Compare the project with the architecture model
where.description: The loans module in kata/step2/java has a folder structure all of its own. Work out how its packages relate to the diagram shown. Do not move a single file during this exercise, because the later exercises rely on the current structure.
where.list.label: Map the packages: open the kata/step2/java folder and list the packages under step2, without opening a single file yet.
where.guess.label: Estimate and verify the contents: decide from the package names alone what each one should hold. Only then open the files and check where your estimate was off.
where.compare.label: Compare with the model: put your list of packages next to the figure above, where some of these packages sit somewhere else.
where.sort.label: Work out the restructuring: write down which packages have to move, where they go, and which parts the diagram has no place for.
where.plan.label: Test the agent's plan: have the agent work out exactly the same restructuring in plan mode. Put its proposed plan next to your own analysis, and explicitly do not approve the plan yet.
fifteen.title: Fifteen minutes, shape only
fifteen.description: Nothing is graded and nothing is submitted. The clock is the only constraint, and the list of details you did not reach is the real answer.
fifteen.clock.label: Set a timer: put fifteen minutes on the clock.
fifteen.pick.label: Pick a subject: choose one feature from these options: a search box over a list, a link shortener or an export button.
fifteen.shape.label: Focus on the basic shape: ask the agent for the bare visual shape only. Deliberately leave out an empty state, validation and progress bars.
fifteen.loop.label: Iterate in small steps: run it, pick one next addition each time and ask for that specific part alone.
fifteen.write.label: Record the unfinished details: when the clock goes off, write down the three details you did not manage to finish.
steer.title: Steer a run
steer.description: All of this runs against kata/step2/java. Nothing is graded and nothing is submitted; the tick is a bookmark.
steer.escape.label: Ask for something under-specified and press Escape while it is still thinking. Run git status. Nothing should have moved.
steer.queue.label: Ask again, and this time type the clarification while it works. Note which turn it lands on.
steer.gap.label: Put the ## Gaps rule in kata/step2/java/CLAUDE.md, then ask for the late fee to be calculated in euros. Check that it stops and writes the question down instead of picking one.
steer.worktree.label: Run git worktree add -b feat/scratch ../kata-scratch, start a second agent in it, then git worktree remove ../kata-scratch. Two folders, one history.
count.title: Count your own hour
count.description: This one runs against your own work, not against the kata. Nothing is graded and nothing is submitted; the tick is a bookmark.
count.time.label: Time one loop on your own project: from asking for a change to seeing it in the running app.
count.fit.label: Work out how many of those fit in an hour, and put your number beside the eleven in the drawing above.
count.tally.label: Take one working day and split the hours between deciding, driving, reading, and typing code yourself.
count.cut.label: Name the single slowest thing in that loop, and say what it would cost to remove it.
gate-walk.title: Analyse your own quality gates
gate-walk.description: You do this exercise on your own day-to-day work, not inside the kata's practice environment. Nothing is graded and nothing is submitted. The tick is only a bookmark for yourself.
gate-walk.list.label: Map the checkpoints: list every checkpoint a change has to pass on its way to production, both human reviews and automated steps.
gate-walk.reach.label: Work out the impact of mistakes: for each checkpoint, write down how far a mistake has already got in the chain by the time that particular point catches it.
gate-walk.time.label: Time the automated steps: measure how long the automated checkpoints take and mark which steps the agent can run on its own inside its own iteration.
gate-walk.goal.label: Name the main bottleneck: pick the slowest automated checkpoint the agent cannot run on its own. Write a goal for it: the turnaround time you want and the quality requirements that may not be sacrificed for it.
audit.row.headers.remark: X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options are set, Content-Security-Policy is not. Fix: add it report-only first, then enforce it.
audit.row.audience.topic: The aud claim on a token
audit.row.audience.remark: The decoder checks the signature and the expiry and never looks at aud, so a token minted for another service in the same realm is accepted. Fix: add an audience validator.
audit.row.errors.remark: The handler puts the exception message in the body. On a constraint violation that prints the column names with it. Fix: log it, return a code.
audit.caption: An example security audit, not a run against this repository.
flow-naive.description: You ask, the agent writes the code inside the project. Nothing is settled between you before it does.
flow-plan.description: You and the agent settle the task between you first, and only then does the agent write the code inside the project.
flow-spec.description: You and the agent settle the task between you first, and the agent then writes the code inside the project, which also holds the spec the code is built from.
flow-defer.description: In this session you and the agent work on the task, and what the agent turns up outside it goes down into findings.md instead of into the work. In a later session you read findings.md, turn it into a spec or a prompt, and hand that to the agent, which changes the code in the project.
flow-audit.description: You ask the agent, the agent writes audit.md, you read it, you hand rows back to the agent, and the agent changes the project, which holds the code and, optionally, a spec. Above the row, an agent audits the changed project again and writes a new version of audit.md. Below it, the changed project also comes back to you: you check the fix and close its row in audit.md.
flow-audit.branch-note: check the fix, close the row
workflow-timeline.naive.name: Naive
workflow-timeline.naive.note: A first version, to find out whether the idea stands up at all.
workflow-timeline.plan-first.name: Plan-based
workflow-timeline.plan-first.note: It stood up, so every change gets planned before it is written.
workflow-timeline.specs.name: Spec-driven
workflow-timeline.specs.note: The features that are staying get a spec each, scope and all.
workflow-timeline.audit.name: Audit-driven
workflow-timeline.audit.note: A reflection on what you built, read against what the specs asked for.
workflow-timeline.plan-fixes.name: Plan/naive
workflow-timeline.plan-fixes.note: One row of the audit at a time. The small ones you fix straight away, the rest you plan.
workflow-timeline.return: what changed goes back into the specs
workflow-weights.description: Four bars of the same length, one per workflow, each cut into what you decide first, what the agent runs, and what you read afterwards. Naive decides almost nothing up front and leaves a long read; spec-driven is the reverse.
loops-per-hour.description: The same hour drawn twice. The first band gets through two turns and the start of a third, almost all of it waiting. The second gets through eleven, with the waiting cut to the size of the other two parts.
skill-shape.description: Two profile shapes. On the left one deep bar and nothing either side. On the right the same bar, the same depth, with a wide crossbar added on top of it.
skill-shape.breadth: enough of the rest to judge it
iteration-paths.description: Two routes from the same start to the same target. On the left, three long steps that stop beside it. On the right, twelve short ones that land in it, and four dropped versions branching off along the way, each aimed at the target and none of them arriving.
iteration-paths.few: Prototyping the old way took weeks
iteration-paths.many: With vibe coding, an agent has it done in an hour
agents-at-once.description: Five arrangements drawn as wires from you to the agents you are running. One agent on a single solid teal wire. Then four agents on four thin dashed ones, none of them teal. Then one teal wire to an agent that holds the wires to the same four itself. Then a dashed wire to a pair of agents joined by a wire that runs both ways. Then one teal wire to an agent in front, with three dashed wires to agents running behind it.
agents-at-once.one.name: One agent
agents-at-once.one.note: one diff, read as it lands
agents-at-once.many.name: Four at once
agents-at-once.many.note: four diffs, all at the end
agents-at-once.orchestrated.name: Four, orchestrated
agents-at-once.orchestrated.note: four runs, one thing to read
agents-at-once.recursive.name: A pair, arguing
agents-at-once.recursive.note: one diff, hours of argument later
agents-at-once.mixed.name: One in front, three behind
agents-at-once.mixed.note: one now, three when they report
script-runs.description: The same request, resetting the database before a demo, run three times and drawn twice. Each run is a card whose three bars are the steps of the reset (dropped, seeded, checked), and a bar's length is how much that step did on that run. Asked in words, the three runs come out different. As one script, the three runs are identical.
script-runs.request: The request, every run: reset the database before a demo
script-runs.legend: bar length: how much that step did on that run
script.title: Write it once
script.description: Something you have typed at an agent more than twice this week. If nothing comes to mind, use starting this step's project and checking what it returns.
script.name.label: Name the repetition. You have already typed one: mvn spring-boot:run in kata/step2/java, then curl -s localhost:8080/api/loans/statement/STUDENT | jq to see what comes back.
script.ask.label: Ask the agent for the script. It picks the language, not you.
script.twice.label: Run it twice and compare the two outputs. Anything that differs is interpretation still left in the script.
script.skill.label: Write a skill beside it whose description says when to call it, in one line.
script.find.label: Open a new session and ask for the job in your own words. If the agent finds the script, the description is doing its work.
two-windows.description: Two context windows side by side. In the left one the wrong file sits in the window in full, with your correction under it and the next turn after that, and all of it is re-sent on every turn. In the right one you rewound to your request in the same session: the request and the wrong file it led to are struck through as dropped, and the window goes on with the rewritten request and the work, so the wrong turn is never sent again.
two-windows.forward.name: Send a correction
two-windows.forward.note: all of it, re-sent every turn
two-windows.rewind.name: Rewind, in the same session
loop-in-window.description: Two context windows side by side. The left one holds four failed fixes and a fifth coming out the same shape, because the failures are the strongest pattern in the window. The right one is a fresh window holding one carried block, the error and the approach that failed, and a fresh attempt with room around it.
loop-in-window.dirty.name: The fifth try
loop-in-window.dirty.note: the loop is in the window
loop-in-window.clean.name: The second try
loop-in-window.clean.note: one thing carried, chosen by you
worktree-each.description: Two checkout folders side by side, kata-statement on the branch feat/statement and kata-native on feat/native, each holding its own agent and its own code. Both connect down to one shared history, and no line runs from one folder to the other.
worktree-each.note: neither can reach the other's files
window-spend.description: One rolling window drawn as columns of spend against a dashed ceiling. Ten ordinary sessions come nowhere near it and the space above them is left empty. The last two columns reach the ceiling.
goal-gate.description: Three boxes in a row. The agent's pass leads into a box holding the command mvn verify, and a green arrow leads from there to the run reporting back. A second path leaves the command box downwards and returns to the pass, labelled red.
read-each-time.description: What each agent is holding. On the left, one agent with three blocks of reading and five pieces of work under them. On the right, five agents, each holding an identical copy of those same three blocks in front of its one piece of work.
read-each-time.extra: the same reading, bought five times
model-relay.description: Three columns joined by two teal arrows. A large block of broad research on Fable, a smaller block of planning on Opus, then five small blocks of work on Sonnet.
walking-skeleton.alt: An early screenshot of this site: black text on white, one step called Warm-up: FizzBuzz in the sidebar, a notes panel, and a box to type an answer into.
walking-skeleton.caption: This is the very first page this repository rendered, before any part of the design system was in place.
added-details.alt: The course as it looks now: a dark teal header carrying the title, a white card holding a grouped sidebar with ticks against finished pages, and a unit set in the design system's typefaces.
added-details.caption: The same course after the details were refined: with the proper header, the final styling and colours, neatly grouped steps and the settings behind the cogwheel.
tree.claude-md.note: read at the start of every session
tree.settings.note: permissions, and where hooks are declared
tree.nested-claude-md.note: read only when the agent works in here
tree.module-claude-md.note: the conventions of that module only
tree.rule.note: read only with a file that matches
domain-tree.domain.note: the rules, and the ports they need
domain-tree.repository-port.note: a port, written by the domain
domain-tree.adapter.note: the outside world, and only here
domain-tree.outgoing.note: what the domain calls out to
domain-tree.controller.note: calls the use case, never the aggregate
domain-tree.properties.note: points Liquibase at the changelog below
domain-tree.test.note: tests mirror the package they cover
domain-tree.author.note: the next domain, same three packages
domain-tree.caption: An example project, not one in this repository.
words-to-files.description: A prompt reading cap the headline at 80 characters, with the word headline picked out. One arrow leads from it to article/Headline.java, the first of three files in the repository. The other two, article/Article.java and author/Author.java, have nothing pointing at them.
hexagon-ports.description: Two hexagons, one inside the other: application around domain. Three adapter boxes on the left send arrows in and three on the right receive arrows out, and every arrow crosses a port sitting on the outer hexagon's edge.
same-gate.description: Two labels, you write and an agent writes, on lines that join into one before they reach a single box holding static analysis, a coverage floor and a mutation score. One arrow leaves that box, to ship.
sdlc-stages.today.name: Today
sdlc-stages.today.body: Six departments and five handovers. The build phase takes the most time and therefore sets the pace of the whole process.
sdlc-stages.assisted.name: AI-assisted
sdlc-stages.assisted.body: Agents build. The bottleneck moves to what you asked for and to whoever checks it.
sdlc-stages.native.name: The AI-native chain
sdlc-stages.native.body: With handovers a thing of the past, the work runs in one smooth flow. Only four human decision points still set the final speed.
sdlc-stages.return: What happens in production feeds the next piece of work
sdlc-stages.legend.waits: Where the run narrows, the work waits
sdlc-stages.caption: After the AI-native SDLC on smartagents.be, which builds on Anthropic's AI-native SDLC playbook.
gate-reach.description: A band running from the file an agent just wrote to production, cut into five regions that widen and darken to the right: file, worktree, branch, main, production. Four teal gates stand between them: unit tests answering in seconds, mvn verify in a minute, CI and your review in minutes, and the release, where a person decides. The further out a gate sits, the slower it answers and the more a miss has reached.
gate-reach.heading: where a change has got to when each gate answers
gate-reach.gate.loop.name: unit tests
gate-reach.gate.done.name: mvn verify
gate-reach.gate.merge.name: CI, your review
gate-reach.gate.release.name: release
gate-reach.note: the further out a gate sits, the slower it answers and the more a miss has reached
quiz.small-change-no-spec.question: Your team keeps one spec file per feature and you follow it. Today's list is a log line in the wrong place and a column that should have been nullable. Writing the specs would take longer than the changes do. What is the right call?
quiz.small-change-no-spec.nudge: Do them the naive way, straight in the code. A change that decides nothing does not earn a workflow.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.consistency: Write the specs anyway. A workflow you apply only when you feel like it stops being a workflow, and the exceptions are where the drift starts.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.batch: Hold the small changes back until there are enough of them to cover in one spec, so the file count stays sensible.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.audit: Make the changes, then run an audit over the repository, which is the pass that catches whatever the small ones broke.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.explanation: A spec is worth writing when something is being decided. A log line and a nullable column decide nothing, so the spec is cost with no answer in it.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.question: You stop asking for changes and start asking for a plan first, every time. The work that comes back is better, which surprises you, because you approve most of the plans with barely an edit. Where did the gain come from?
quiz.plan-mode-interview.interview: The plan interviewed you. Its questions were the decisions you had skipped, and you answered them before a line of code existed.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.thinking: The model reasons for longer before it writes, and that extra thinking comes back to you as a better first draft.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.document: The plan stays in the repository beside the code, so the next session starts from what this one decided.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.review: Reading a plan is faster than reading a diff, so you catch the mistakes earlier and it costs you less to say no.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.explanation: You approve most plans because answering the questions was the work. The agent asks which tier gets a grace period and what happens when the list comes back empty, and the workflow puts you back in the design.
quiz.audit-as-essay.question: You ask an agent whether a module is complete, secure and consistent with the rest of the repository. Back come four pages of prose. You read it once, agree with most of it, and a week later you cannot remember which parts you dealt with. What went wrong?
quiz.audit-as-essay.format: You did not ask for a format. A table keeps it to what you can act on, and it lives in the repository, so next week it still says which row you were on.
quiz.audit-as-essay.scope: You asked about three things at once. Run completeness, security and style as separate passes and each answer comes back short enough to act on.
quiz.audit-as-essay.memory: The session ended and the reading went with it. Paste the report back in at the start of the next one and carry on from where it stopped.
quiz.audit-as-essay.model: Prose is what a model falls back on when it is not confident. A narrower question would have got you a narrower answer.
quiz.audit-as-essay.explanation: An audit is a file in your repository, so it diffs and gets reviewed the way the code does. Ask for the topic, where it lives, how solid it is and what to do about it, and you have rows to work rather than paragraphs to re-read.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.question: You hand an agent a module nobody has touched in years, with one line: make this code cleaner and keep the tests green. Four hours and a small fortune in tokens later it reports that the work is done. The diff is enormous and the code looks about the same. What went wrong?
quiz.report-on-a-wish.no-command: Nothing could say the work was done. Green tests say what must not change, not when to stop, so the run stopped when it felt finished.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.too-long: The run was too long to hold together. Broken into four one-hour goals it would have kept its bearings and each piece would have landed.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.wrong-tier: The tier was wrong for the job. Refactoring is judgement work, and a cheaper model spends a long run rewriting rather than deciding.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.no-worktree: It ran on your branch. Working next to your own edits, it kept rereading files that were changing under it and lost track of what it had done.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.explanation: A goal is a task with an outcome something else can measure, and "cleaner" is not one. Name the command that prints the answer, a coverage floor or a complexity ceiling, and the run has something to run until.
quiz.fleet-bill.question: You have five specs written, so you fan them out across five agents instead of working through them yourself. Everything lands inside the hour, which is what you wanted. The token bill is several times what the same five jobs cost last month, done one after another in one session. Where did it go?
quiz.fleet-bill.read-again: Every agent started on an empty context, so every one of them read its way into the project again before it wrote anything.
quiz.fleet-bill.overwrote: The agents worked the same files at the same time, so a good part of the run was work being written over and done a second time.
quiz.fleet-bill.gathered: Everything the agents produced was gathered back into one window at the end, and that transcript is re-sent on every turn after it.
quiz.fleet-bill.pricier-tier: A fan-out runs on the top tier by default, because coordinating several agents is the kind of work the cheaper tiers cannot hold together.
quiz.fleet-bill.explanation: Every agent pays again for the same CLAUDE.md, the same files and the same reasoning, and none of them learns from the others. That is the trade: you buy wall-clock time with tokens.
quiz.window-tail.question: You are on a subscription that meters you in a rolling five-hour window. Everything you cared about today is finished and reviewed, and there are thirty-five minutes of window left. What is the best use of them?
quiz.window-tail.spend-it: Start something expensive you wanted anyway. A design pass or a fleet against specs you already wrote, so the tail goes on real work instead of expiring.
quiz.window-tail.save-it: Leave it. What you do not spend rolls into the next window, so a quiet afternoon is what buys you a heavy morning tomorrow.
quiz.window-tail.stop-early: Stop working and let the window turn over early, so the next one starts clean instead of half spent when you need it.
quiz.window-tail.upgrade-small: Put the small jobs left on your list on the frontier model. The window is paid for either way, so the highest tier is the one to spend it at.
quiz.window-tail.explanation: Unspent window does not carry over, so the tail of one is the cheapest moment for a move you were going to make sooner or later. Spending it at a higher tier on work that never needed one buys nothing.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.question: Your request was ambiguous and the agent has opened the wrong file. It has not written anything yet. What do you do?
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.rewind: Go back to your request, rewrite it, and let it start again.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.correct-: Send a correction naming the right file.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.clear: Escape, then clear the session and start over.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.queue: Queue the correction so it picks it up on the next turn.
quiz.wrong-turn-nothing-written.explanat: Nothing has been written, so a rewind costs nothing and takes the wrong turn out of the window. A correction leaves the wrong file in the window for the rest of the session.
quiz.third-correction.question: You have told the agent three times this week to stop putting a summary paragraph at the end of every file it touches. It fixes it each time, and the next file comes back with one. What has gone wrong?
quiz.third-correction.no-home: The correction only lives in messages you retype, so nothing carries it to the next session.
quiz.third-correction.context-full: The window filled up, so the instruction was pushed out partway through.
quiz.third-correction.wrong-model: The tier is too small to hold an instruction that specific.
quiz.third-correction.prompt-wording: The instruction is worded loosely, so it has to be phrased more precisely.
quiz.third-correction.explanation: A correction you repeat is knowledge with no home yet. Written into a skill it is a file in the repository, so the next session starts with it.
quiz.skill-still-off.question: Your commit-message skill works. The messages still come back wrong in the same small way, and you have just repaired one by hand. What do you do with the repair?
quiz.skill-still-off.both-versions: Give the agent its version and yours, and ask what the skill failed to say.
quiz.skill-still-off.longer-prompt: Put the missing rule in your next prompt, where the agent is sure to read it.
quiz.skill-still-off.stricter-descriptio: Tighten the skill's description so it fires more often.
quiz.skill-still-off.rewrite-skill: Rewrite the skill from scratch, since a rule producing the same mistake is the wrong rule.
quiz.skill-still-off.explanation: The repair is the rule the skill is missing, and the agent can name it from the two versions. Writing that answer back is the pass that makes the skill sound like you.
quiz.script-or-skill.question: Before every demo you clean the database, seed three members and start the service, and you explain the steps to the agent each time. It gets there, and each run leaves the data slightly different. What is worth writing?
quiz.script-or-skill.script-and-skill: A script that does the steps, and a skill that calls it so the agent knows it exists.
quiz.script-or-skill.longer-skill: A skill with the steps written out, since the agent can run the commands.
quiz.script-or-skill.claude-md: A line in CLAUDE.md naming the steps, so it is read on every turn.
quiz.script-or-skill.plan-mode: A plan, so the agent works the steps out once and follows its own plan each run.
quiz.script-or-skill.explanation: Steps that must end in the same state every time belong in a script. The skill beside it is only what makes the agent aware the script is there.
quiz.deep-not-wide.question: You have the afternoon and one thing on your mind: what the entities in a new feature are, and which of them owns the late-fee rule. You have not settled any of it yet. Which arrangement do you reach for?
quiz.deep-not-wide.one-agent: One agent and one conversation, and you read every step of it.
quiz.deep-not-wide.four-drafts: Four agents, each drafting a different domain model, and you keep the best one.
quiz.deep-not-wide.front-and-behind: One agent in front on the model, three behind writing the tests for it.
quiz.deep-not-wide.orchestrated: One agent that decomposes the design and briefs sub-agents on the pieces.
quiz.deep-not-wide.explanation: The decision is the work here, and you make it in a conversation you read every step of. Nothing behind you can start on a model that is not settled yet.
quiz.green-and-unread.question: Four agents have run all afternoon on four modules, each in its own worktree. All four builds are green. You have four diffs open and you have read two of them properly. How should you read that afternoon?
quiz.green-and-unread.reading-at-the-end: The steering you skipped at the start arrived at the end as reading, and the fourth diff gets less of you than the first did.
quiz.green-and-unread.builds-are-the-che: Nothing has gone wrong: the builds are the check, and all four passed.
quiz.green-and-unread.window-too-small: The agents ran out of context, so the later work is worse than the early work.
quiz.green-and-unread.shared-branch: They should have shared one branch, so the changes merged as they were written.
quiz.green-and-unread.explanation: Running four at once means you stop steering and start receiving. A green build says the checks passed, not that you got the code you wanted, and attention runs out well before the tokens do.
quiz.who-holds-the-wires.question: Instead of opening five sessions yourself, you brief one agent and it hands five pieces to sub-agents. What does that change?
quiz.who-holds-the-wires.coordination-mo: The coordination moves into the agent, and five runs come back to you as one thing to read.
quiz.who-holds-the-wires.inherits-contex: The sub-agents carry on from your session, so each needs less briefing than a fresh one would.
quiz.who-holds-the-wires.answer-each: You get more control per piece, because you can answer each sub-agent while it works.
quiz.who-holds-the-wires.runs-in-turn: The pieces run one after another rather than at once, so none of them can collide.
quiz.who-holds-the-wires.explanation: A sub-agent starts on an empty context with its brief and nothing else, and it answers to the agent that briefed it rather than to you. You stop holding the five pieces together yourself.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.question: Four fixes in, the test fails the way it failed the first time, and the agent's latest fix undoes the one before it. What now?
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.clear-and-carr: Stop, clear, and start again carrying the error and the approach that failed.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.rewind: Go back to the message that started the run and rewrite it.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.tell-it: Tell it the last four attempts did not work and to try something else.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.paste-output: Paste the failing test output in and let it keep going.
quiz.fifth-fix-same-shape.explanation: The message was fine, so rewinding puts you back into the same run. The four failed attempts are the strongest pattern in the window, and only a clear removes them.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.question: Your CLAUDE.md carries the standing Gaps rule. The agent comes back with a diff and three entries in gaps.md. What went wrong? It comes back with a diff and three entries in gaps.md. What went wrong?
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.should-have-s: It should have stopped and asked. The diff is built on the guesses.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.nothing-wrong: Nothing. It followed the rule and you have the list.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.wrong-place: The rule belongs in the prompt rather than in CLAUDE.md.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.commit-messag: The entries belong in the commit message, where the reviewer reads them next to the diff.
quiz.logged-and-carried-on.explanation: Log a gap and build on it anyway, and you get a list of guesses under a diff that already depends on them. Stopping is the part of the rule that matters.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.question: You want a rough module turned into something you would put your name on, and you are in meetings all afternoon. You brief one agent to build it, have it spawn a harsh critic, and tell the pair to keep going until the critic has no remarks left. What are you buying?
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.rounds-you-skip: The rounds of review you would have done yourself, paid for in tokens and hours instead of in your attention.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.two-are-faster: A faster result than one agent alone, because two agents split the work between them.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.signed-off: A diff you no longer have to read, because the critic has already signed it off.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.steer-as-it-goes: A run you can steer, because you answer the critic's remarks as they come in.
quiz.pair-buys-rounds.explanation: One diff comes back, carrying the last word of an argument you took no part in, and you still read it.
